# Heliocentric model (`heliocentrism`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: needs round_earth_size; helped by telescope, laws_of_motion, keplers_laws
- Core idea: The Earth turns on its axis once a day and travels round the Sun once a year, as the third of the planets; only the Moon goes round the Earth. This explains at one stroke why the planets sometimes move backwards (the Earth overtakes them), why Mercury and Venus never stray far from the Sun, and the order and relative distances of the planets. Evidence with a small telescope: Venus shows a full set of phases like the Moon and changes size, so it circles the Sun; Jupiter has four moons, so not everything circles the Earth. We do not feel the motion because everything on Earth shares it.
- Pitfalls:
  - Claiming Copernicus's system predicted better or was simpler; with circles it still needed epicycles and was no more accurate than Ptolemy
  - Having no answer to the serious objections: no visible shift of the stars through the year (they are immensely far) and no wind or falling behind (inertia)
  - Presenting the phases of Venus as proof; they refute Ptolemy but also fit Tycho's system, in which the planets circle a Sun that circles the Earth
  - Saying the Sun is the fixed centre of the universe
  - Underestimating the religious and legal risk after 1616, or inventing it before
- History: greece: c. 270 BC Aristarchus of Samos; c. 150 BC Seleucus of Seleucia defends it; rejected by Hipparchus and Ptolemy; india: 499 – Aryabhata teaches the daily rotation of the Earth (his planetary model stays geocentric); islamic: 13th–14th c. al-Tusi and Ibn al-Shatir devise the geometrical tools Copernicus later uses, in geocentric models; Earth's rotation debated by al-Biruni and at Maragha; europe: 1543 Copernicus, De revolutionibus; 1609–1619 Kepler; 1610 Galileo's telescope observations; 1616 Copernicus's book suspended, 1633 Galileo's trial; 1728 Bradley's aberration, first direct proof of the Earth's motion; 1838 Bessel's stellar parallax; 1851 Foucault's pendulum shows the rotation
- Read:
  - Nicolaus Copernicus, De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (1543)
  - Galileo Galilei, Dialogo sopra i due massimi sistemi del mondo (1632)
  - Thomas S. Kuhn, The Copernican Revolution (1957)
